assumptions: The 14:14Z deploy was treated as the leading suspect on timing alone; its contents were never retrieved, so its involvement is assumed, not shown.
The alert start time is taken as the user-visible start of impact; logs show latency already climbing at 14:15, so real impact likely began slightly earlier than the alert.
Recovery at 14:20 is assumed to be self-resolution, since no mitigating action was taken and nothing in the evidence explains the return to normal. It may recur.

The retrieved metrics and logs are assumed to represent the whole service; the log lines available were generic latency/timeout messages with no endpoint, dependency or error detail, and the same small set was returned on every query.
The absence of recent feature-flag changes in the provider's history is assumed to mean no flag change was involved.
The draft pull request is assumed to be unvalidated: it was generated after investigation stalled and addresses a cause that was never confirmed.
input.executive_summary: On 17 September 2026, an online service that handles customer requests became slow and then began timing out. The problem started at about 14:17 UTC, when monitoring first fired, with the first warning signs about a minute or two earlier; service returned to normal at about 14:20 UTC, roughly three minutes later. During that window some customer requests were slower than usual and a portion of them failed outright rather than completing; the measured share of affected traffic is recorded with the incident metrics and was not re-derived here. Automated responders investigated three times over, reviewing recent metrics, log lines, deployment history and feature-flag history. They found no change they could safely and reversibly undo, so no corrective action was taken, and the service recovered on its own. Because no cause could be confirmed from the evidence available, the incident was escalated to human engineers, with a draft code change opened for review as a starting point rather than as a verified fix. Follow-up should focus on why the service recovered, since that remains unexplained.
input.root_cause: Not established. The only change on record for io-shop was a deploy of revision 9f4c1e7b2a3d5c8e1f0b6a4d2c9e7b5a3f1d8c6e at 14:14Z, and p95 latency began climbing the following minute (220ms baseline -> 900ms -> 1800ms -> 5000ms timeouts), but the link is purely temporal: no diff for that revision, no dependency or code path named in the logs, and no flag changes were found. A downstream/dependency slowdown or resource saturation coinciding with the deploy was never ruled out, and the service recovered on its own without any mitigating action being taken.
